# Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta (Snp 4.2 (PTS Snp 151))

**ID:** Snp 4.2 (PTS Snp 151)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta* ("Eight on the Cave") is the second discourse of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* [Hazra 1994]. It is one of only four poems in the collection that strictly fulfills the definition of an "octave" (*aṭṭhaka*), consisting of eight stanzas (verses 772–779 in the PTS edition) [Hazra 1994; Anderson & Smith 1913; Müller 1881]. The sutta focuses on attachment to the body (the "cave"), sensual pleasures, and notions of "mine," warning that those steeped in them find it difficult to transcend the fear of death and future becoming [Anderson & Smith 1913]. The text urges the sage (*muni*) to understand sensory contact (*phassa*) without greed, remove the arrow of passion, overcome clinging to what is seen or heard, and remain detached from dogmatic disputes and inclinations [Müller 1881; Ruegg & Schmithausen 1990; Ñāṇananda].

Scholars have devoted attention to its metrical and linguistic characteristics. G. C. Pande observes that the four *Aṭṭhaka* poems employ a mixture of Indravajrā and Upendravajrā metres and contain archaic linguistic forms such as *cutāse* and *avītataṇhāse* [Pande 1974]. However, Tilmann Vetter and contributors in David Seyfort Ruegg and Lambert Schmithausen's volume suggest on metrical grounds that the *Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta* (alongside the *Kāma* and *Jarā* suttas) may stem from a later stratum than other poems of the *Aṭṭhakavagga*, with verse 778 reflecting a stage of advanced doctrinal assimilation regarding the transcendence of apperception [Vetter 1988; Ruegg & Schmithausen 1990].

 Within the Pali canon, the sutta is preserved with an extensive word-by-word commentary in the *Guhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa* (*Mahāniddesa* 2) and cited in the *Peṭakopadesa*. DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal reuse with the *Mahāniddesa* across 40 matching segments [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus also match verses of the text with Tibetan works, notably the *Gurulekha* (D 4186), the *Udānavarga* (D 4099, D 0326), and the *Āryamañjuśrīnāmasaṃgītiṭīkā* (D 2534) [DharmaNexus].
